body.text: Millions of Australians were unable to use their Outlook emails during the Microsoft outage that spanned most of the day on Friday.
This halted business operations, interrupted workdays and made everyday online actions extremely difficult for many.
But if you're expecting to be compensated for the headaches the outage brought, don't expect a big cash payout.
Could we be compensated for the Microsoft outage?
Yes, but it will probably just be businesses, RMIT Associate Professor Mark Gregory says.
Dr Gregory says a service level agreement that businesses have with providers such as Microsoft will often have requirements that certain targets are met.
This could be something like the service being fully operational for 99.49 per cent of the year.
"Some of these agreements have mechanisms for compensation if the targets are not met," Dr Gregory says.
"The typical scenario though is that the compensation is in terms of returning a percentage of the monthly or annual fee for using that service.
"It doesn't normally extend to lost productivity."
Microsoft's agreements would only cover the loss of that service, but not the knock-on effects of that, Deakin IT lecturer Fariha Jaigirdar says.
"The loss of productivity is not something they are bound to compensate for," Dr Jaigirdar.
And this compensation is generally made in terms of a credit, which could equate to a small discount on the company's next bill.
"If people are expecting [that] cash will be in their account … that is not something that is going to happen," Dr Jaigirdar says.
It's unclear how Microsoft will address calls for compensation in the coming days, with the global nature of the outage putting pressure on the technology giant to repair its reputation.
The ABC has contacted Microsoft for comment.
How much could the credit be?
There isn't one dollar figure that would apply to every business, Dr Jaigirdar says
This all depends on how much a business pays for its Microsoft services.
And this also depends on whether a business can successfully file a compensation claim with Microsoft, which requires certain information to process compensation.
While larger companies with legal departments might have in-house experts to make a claim, the process could be tricky for smaller businesses to navigate, Dr Jaigirdar says.
"I don't think it's a very straightforward process," she says.
Credit won't cover losses
While a credit towards a monthly bill couldn't hurt, it could be a drop in the ocean compared with what some businesses lost on Friday.
"The credit is tiny compared with the loss of productivity," Dr Gregory says.
"It's a bit like when there's a telco outage, people ultimately just have to wear it and move on."
Dr Gregory says providers such as Microsoft might argue that it's up to businesses to sort out productivity insurance and have alternative workarounds during outages, but it's not that simple.
He says that may well be the case for preparing for things such as telecommunications outages, by having another SIM card, for example.
"[But] with IT and with software, it's not so easy," Dr Gregory says.
"It's not something that you can easily duplicate.
"That argument, to some extent, does not hold water."
What could the ACCC do?
"There is potential for the ACCC to weigh in on the matter, the problem is of course under what section of the act," Dr Gregory says.
There were changes to the legislation that permitted the ACCC to take action against companies that provide telecommunications services.
That legislation was fairly broad.
"[But] that would be in terms of a legal action over the outage, not in relation to compensation," Dr Gregory says.
What about a class action?

"It's a question of really what the purpose of the class action is and whether or not they would try to go beyond the loss of service compensation to loss of productively compensation," Dr Gregory says.
"There may be law firms that want to go to court to just see where the limits are.
"Sometimes this is positive because then it makes it clear about the strengths or weaknesses of current legislation."
The ABC is aware of at least one legal firm investigating the potential for a class action lawsuit over the outage.
Victoria Peak Litigation Funding is currently putting the call out for businesses and individuals who may have suffered financial losses as a result of the outage.
However, the firm is careful to stress that registering to take part "does not establish entitlement to compensation or mean that proceedings have commenced".
And even if a class action does get off the ground and is successful, it can take quite a while until participants see any money.
Calls for automated compensation
Dr Gregory says this saga highlights the need for tougher legislation about how people are compensated when big providers — such as Microsoft — fail.
"The Australian government does need to look at automated compensation," he says.
"But also strengthening sovereign capability so that things like outages outside Australia don't impact productivity inside Australia."
While Dr Jaigirdar doesn't expect changes to be made to legislation overnight, she's hopeful it will prompt action.
"This is adding serious fuel to the regulatory fire in our country," she says.
"Platforms are no longer just office software, they are essential national infrastructure — no different from telecommunications and water.
"It needs to be taken seriously."
She also called for a national alert system to inform the community about similar outages in the future.
